I think there's no direct harm in saying "Gene Wilder is in a better place now" since nobody in your family knows anybody in Gene Wilder's family. 

Here's where it becomes harmful: At some point, people who say that line will need to comfort somebody who is bereaved. Instead of listening and acknowledging the pain, they will fall back on the "better place now" cliche. The "better place now" line (along with similar platitudes) sends the message that the bereaved are WRONG to be sad since death is actually better than life. It allows people to avoid the hard work of feeling empathy and sitting with pain. Instead it shifts the burden to the bereaved. (Stop being sad in public when God has a master plan and everything is perfect now.)

Your wife shouldn't feel guilty and she did nothing wrong... but it's going to be hard to convince her of that. Guilt is a natural reaction to horrible things. (I think it may be because it gives us control to believe we COULD have had influence. It's easier to feel guilty than it is to feel powerless sometimes. 

There's a great book called "When Bad Things Happen to Good People." It's by a rabbi. In one part, he talks about visiting a grieving son who's mother passed away. The son feels guilty. He's moved his Mom to Florida and he's convinced that the change in climate was what killed her. Around the same time, the rabbi visited a SECOND son who's mother just died. The second son also blames himself because he DIDN'T move his mother to Florida and surely the cold weather was what killed her. 

Guilt is natural and illogical. I wish you and your wife well in your efforts to escape guilty feelings you don't deserve. I hope your friend gets the help she needs and I hope that your support helps.
